results.title: Establishing the Minimal Clinically Important Difference and Substantial Clinical Benefit for the Pain Visual Analog Scale in a Postoperative Hand Surgery Population - PMC
results.content: The two main techniques for calculating MCID are 1) anchor-based and 2) distribution-based.5 Both of these methods have been utilized recently in the hand surgery literature to aid in the interpretation of clinical outcomes scores.6–13 Anchor-based methods are useful because they query patients directly for a global rating of change, which is then used in MCID estimations.14 Distribution-based methods can account for change beyond some level of random variation and have been widely utilized across fields within the medical literature.10,15–19 However, limitations of the distribution-based method include having few agreed-upon benchmarks for establishing clinically relevant improvement, and lack of including the patient’s perspective of clinically important change.14,20 Whereas MCID describes the smallest change in a clinical outcome that a patient considers meaningful, SCB describes the value for substantial improvement, or the amount of quantifiable outcome improvement that is needed for a patient to feel substantially better.4,21. It cannot be assumed that VAS-pain MCID and SCB values for hand surgery patients are the same as those described in other populations such as shoulder surgery patients,22–28 Therefore, the primary purpose of our study was estimate the MCID for VAS-pain in a postoperative non-shoulder hand and upper extremity surgery population using anchor-based and 1/2 standard deviation (SD) methods. Consistent with recent hand surgery literature, MCID was estimated using the 1/2 SD method and an anchor-based approach.6–13 The 1/2 SD MDIC estimate was calculated as previously described, taking into account both the baseline and follow-up scores.6–9 Anchor-based MCID estimates were calculated using the difference in the mean score change between anchor groups reporting “No change” and the combined group reporting low levels of improvement (“Slightly Improved” and “Improved”) on the pain-specific anchor question, as previously described.6 As such, the resulting anchor-based MCID values are reflective of minimally important improvement, as we did not include the “slightly worse” and “worse” groups in our calculation. In summary, we have derived MCID and SCB estimates for the VAS-pain instrument in a non-shoulder hand and upper extremity postoperative patient population through commonly utilized methods, including anchor-based (MCID and SCB), 1/2 SD (MCID), and ROC methods.

results.title: Clinical Utility of Patient-Reported Outcome Measurement Information System Domain Scales | Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes
results.content: The use of a continuous linear scale and normalized distribution may increase sensitivity to change over time in outcomes in response to treatment and improve statistical power to detect differences across treatment groups as compared to traditional clinician-reported measures.11 Previous investigations of PROMIS tools support their feasibility to assess outcomes in patients with ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke.12,13 The availability of these measures provides the opportunity to improve our understanding of outcomes after stroke and increase the sophistication in which outcome measures are used in clinical care and research. Anchor-based approaches involve comparing PRO scores to a clinically-relevant anchor, or external measure, whereas distribution-based methods rely on the statistical distributions of the PRO.23 Anchor-based methods have been recommended as the primary approach to evaluate meaningful change in PROMs with the use of distribution-based methods as a secondary approach to provide additional evidence supporting the determined values.16,24 A patient-reported global rating of change is the most commonly utilized anchor-based method for estimating the MID.25 We estimated the MID using an external measure of change, the PGIC question, completed within 6 months of the stroke. Measurement error is not consistent across the continuum of scores for an instrument, with estimates being more reliable near the midrange of the scale and less so at either extreme.30 To evaluate whether estimates differed across the range of scores, we calculated MIDs by baseline PROMIS scores indicating good, fair, and severe health-related quality of life (defined as ≥45, 40–44, <40, respectively, for physical function and social role satisfaction; and ≤55, 56–60, >60, respectively, for anxiety and fatigue). Anchor-based MIDs, defined by patients who indicated improvement (minimally improved or much improved) ranged from an average change of 2.4 (±8.3) T-score points for fatigue, to 3.5 (±10.0) for anxiety, 4.0 (±7.4) for physical function, and 6.2 (±8.5) for social role satisfaction (Table 2 and 4). A study of 148 patients presenting for spine surgery found MID estimates were highest for PROMIS fatigue (5.8 T-score points) and anxiety (5.7) and lower for physical function (4.5) and satisfaction with participation in social roles (4.4).28 Kozlowski et al29 found somewhat opposite results in a sample of patients with neurological conditions, including stroke.

results.title: Outcome measures in chronic low back pain - PMC
results.content: The purpose of this prospective, single site cohort quasi-experimental study was to determine the responsiveness of the numerical rating scale (NRS), Roland–Morris disability questionnaire (RMDQ), Oswestry disability index (ODI), pain self-efficacy questionnaire (PSEQ) and the patient-specific functional scale (PSFS) in order to determine which would best measure clinically meaningful change in a chronic low back pain (LBP) population. Based on ROC curve analysis the PSFS and PSEQ were more responsive than the other scales in measuring change in patients with chronic LBP following participation in a back class programme. **Keywords:** Low back pain, Outcome measures, Minimally clinically important change, Responsiveness, Functional assessment, Clinical significance, Patient-reported outcomes. Patient global impression of change (PGIC) has been recommended by the initiative on methods, measurement, and pain assessment in clinical trials (IMMPACT) for use in chronic pain clinical trials as a core outcome measure of global improvement with treatment [19]. As such, the purpose of this study was twofold: first, to demonstrate the responsiveness of five different questionnaires PSFS, PSEQ, NRS, ODI and the RMDQ (using both anchor- and distribution-based methods) and second, to compare which of these tools best measures change in patients with chronic LBP following participation in a back class programme. *RMDQ* Roland–Morris disability questionnaire (score 0–24); *ODI* Oswestry disability index score (0–100); *NRS* numerical rating scale (score 0–10); *PSEQ* pain self-efficacy questionnaire (score 0–60); *PSFS* patient-specific functional scale score (0–10); *SEM* standard error of measurement; *SDC* smallest detectable change; *MCID* minimal clinical important difference; *AUC* area under the curve. In this current investigation, score changes in the five different questionnaires were subjected to both distribution- and anchor-based methods: standard error of measurement (SEM) and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves to define clinical improvement. Based on ROC curve analysis, the PSFS and PSEQ were more responsive than the NRS, RMDQ and ODI to detect clinically important change in patients with chronic LBP. Patient global impression of change (PGIC) has been recommended by IMMPACT [19] for use in chronic pain clinical trials as a core outcome measure of global improvement with treatment and has been extensively used as a comparison in much of the literature regarding responsiveness.

results.title: R: Determination of the Minimal Clinically Important Difference...
results.content: Determination of the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) ### Description A function to calculate the MCID for one dimension of health-related quality of life using the Anchor-based method. ### Usage ### Arguments `score_1`the Post-test score of each dimension `score_2`the Pre-test score if we calculate the MCID without Response shift effect, and it is the Then-test score in the case of MCID with Response shift effect of each dimension `X`the Jaeschke's question with five categories ### Details This function calculates the MCID with and without effect of response shift for the 5 categories cited in the Jaeschke's question (much worse (MW), little worse (LW), no change (NC), little better (LB), much better (MB)) for each quality of life dimension in oncology using the "Anchor-based method". The MCID is the Mean difference between Post-test and Pre-test if we calculate the MCID without effect of response shift and the Mean difference between Post-test and Then-test if we calculate the MCID with effect of response shift for each category of QoL dimension. More concretely, for example if we want to calculate the MCID with effect of Response shift at (T1) used the data (dataghs), we calculate the difference between the two variables GHS1 and GHSr1, then we calculate the average of the values associated for the category (MW) in the variable anchor1, in this case we obtain the MCID for the category much worse, and the MCID for each other category is calculated by the same method. ### Value The values returned by this function are the following: MW: the MCID of the category "much worse" LW: the MCID of the category "little worse" NC: the MCID of the category "no change" LB: the MCID of the category "little better" MB: the MCID of the category "much better" ### Note If we have more than five categories in the Jaeschke's question, we must recode this variable to obtain in the end five categories to implement this function. ### Author(s) ### Examples #Example to calculate the MCID without effect of Response Sift: MCID(dataghs$GHS1, dataghs$GHS0, dataghs$anchor1) #Example to calculate the MCID with effect of Response Sift: MCID(dataghs$GHS1, dataghs$GHSr1, dataghs$anchor1) Package _MRQoL_ version 1.0 [Index]

results.title: Clinimetrics corner: a closer look at the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) - PMC
results.content: Minimal clinically important difference (MCID) scores are commonly used by clinicians when determining patient response to treatment and to guide clinical decision-making during the course of treatment. The minimal clinically important difference (MCID) score is defined as the minimal amount of change that is important to the patient.6 The ability to define a stable, universal MCID score for a particular instrument is an attractive concept for several reasons. The advantage of the anchor-based approach is that change in the outcome measure score is linked to a meaningful external anchor that accounts for the patient’s perspective.3 Most commonly, the global rating of change score is used to define the MCID when attempting to identify change within a patient.3,8 This is clinically relevant for the clinician who wants to understand if the intervention was effective over an episode of care. One of the more common distribution-based change indices is the minimal detectable change (MDC), which is considered the minimal amount of change that is not likely to be due to random variation in measurement.11 However, the MDC alone does not provide information regarding the clinical significance of this change.11 Mintken *et al.*12 reported an MCID of 8 percentage points and an MDC of 11·2 percentage points for the QuickDASH demonstrating that the MCID can be less or greater than the MDC given that one is calculated as a statistical threshold (MDC) while the other is based on a patient response-anchored method (MCID). Terwee *et al.*13 demonstrate this situation perfectly when they describe the large variation in reported MCID scores for a single outcome scale, in one patient group, in one study, at one follow-up when using multiple methods. However, given Jaeschke’s original definition of clinically meaningful change as ‘the smallest difference in score in the domain of interest which patients perceive as beneficial…’, the authors agree with others that MCID estimates should be based upon patient perspective using anchor-based methods.3,17,18 Methods failing to acknowledge the patient’s perspective of clinical significance
